title: Campaign: queues and the outbox across the estate
_note: rv2 S2 (PLAN §2.2 campaign-<tag> row, tag queues-outbox). Sources are 3 live campaign study quests from different repos per idea; recapAfter = any 3 sources passed. Server-local side file, never stamped.

ideas.idea: Write the state change and the message announcing it in one database transaction (the outbox); a separate relay publishes the stored messages.
ideas.why: Saving and then publishing separately loses the message if the process dies in between, or announces a change that was rolled back.
ideas.prompt: A service saves a ticket, then publishes 'ticket.updated' to a broker. After a crash, a customer never gets their notification, and once a notification went out for an update that failed. Explain and fix.
ideas.answer: The two writes can split either way: crash after the save loses the event, publish before a rollback announces a change that never happened. Insert an outbox row in the same transaction as the change; a relay reads committed rows, publishes them and marks them sent. A crash then only delays publishing.

ideas.idea: A worker claims a job with one conditional update (status still queued, a new claim token, attempt count up) and processes it only if that update changed exactly one row.
ideas.why: Read-then-update claims let two workers take the same job, and a worker that lost its lease can still finish and overwrite the new owner's result.
ideas.prompt: Two worker processes poll the same jobs table and sometimes both send the same invoice email. Each one selects a queued job, then updates its status. Fix the claim.
ideas.answer: Make the claim a single UPDATE with the job id and 'status = queued' in the WHERE clause, setting running, a fresh claim token and attempts + 1; continue only if one row changed. When finishing, check the token again so a worker whose lease expired cannot overwrite the result.

ideas.idea: A queue or outbox needs a process that drains it automatically, with retries scheduled by an available-at time and a cap on attempts.
ideas.why: An outbox drained only by a manual endpoint quietly fills up, and a failed row with no retry time is either retried in a hot loop or never again.
ideas.prompt: A webhook outbox is processed only when an admin calls a dispatch endpoint, and failed rows stay failed forever. What two changes make it production-shaped?
ideas.answer: Run a worker that polls on a schedule (or is woken by new rows) and drains in batches. On failure, set an available-at time with growing backoff and count attempts; select rows whose time has come and whose attempts are under the cap, and move exhausted ones aside for a person to inspect.

ideas.idea: A message being processed is hidden for a visibility window; if work takes longer or the ack is lost, it is delivered again, so handlers must tolerate repeats.
ideas.why: A visibility window shorter than the work produces duplicate processing under normal load, not only during failures.
ideas.prompt: A queue's visibility timeout is 30 seconds and some jobs take 45. Customers receive duplicate exports. Explain the mechanism and two fixes.
ideas.answer: After 30 seconds without an ack the message becomes visible again and a second consumer starts it while the first is still working. Extend the visibility while working (or set it above the worst-case time), and make the handler idempotent by job id, so a redelivery that does slip through does no harm.

ideas.idea: Record a run's progress durably as it goes, so a crash mid-run leaves something to resume or dead-letter instead of nothing at all.
ideas.why: A run saved only at the end vanishes when it crashes halfway, so nobody knows which steps already had side effects.
ideas.prompt: A flow engine writes the run record only after all steps finish. A deploy kills a run after step 3 of 6. What do you know about that run afterwards, and what should the engine do instead?
ideas.answer: Nothing: there is no record, so you cannot tell whether steps 1-3 sent emails or charges, and nothing resumes it. Persist the run and each step's state as it starts and completes, so a restarted worker can resume from the last finished step, or dead-letter the run with its history for a person.
